o: Index i is dominant if nums[i] exceeds the average of all elements to its right; the last index never qualifies. Comparing against an average invites floating point; instead compare nums[i] * count > suffixSum, which is exact. For [5,4,3]: index 0 beats average 3.5, index 1 beats 3, answer 2. For [4,1,2]: only index 0 qualifies, answer 1. With n <= 100 even brute force passes, but a suffix-sum sweep is cleaner.
k: nums[i] > avg(suffix) is equivalent to nums[i] * len(suffix) > sum(suffix) — avoids floating point entirely.
One right-to-left pass maintaining a running suffix sum suffices.

a.i: For each i, sum the suffix directly and compare scaled values. O(n^2) is fine for n <= 100.
s: For each i from 0 to n-2, compute the suffix sum.
Count i where nums[i] * (n-1-i) > suffix sum.

a.i: Walk from the last index backward, accumulating the suffix sum; when at index i-1 the accumulated sum is exactly the sum of elements right of i-1, so one comparison finishes the job in O(n).
s: For i from n-1 down to 1: add nums[i] to suf.
If nums[i-1] * (n - i) > suf, increment ans.

w: Always prefer the cross-multiplied integer comparison over doubles to dodge precision bugs. Edge cases: single-element array returns 0; all-equal arrays return 0 since equality is not dominance. Follow-up: dominant over prefix averages, or over max/min of the suffix — same sweep pattern applies.
